items.title: The Outer Loop, Insights First: An Ambient Quality Agent That Diagnoses Your Production Agent How do you keep improving an AI agent after the first 80%, once it serves real product
items.content:
The Outer Loop, Insights First: An Ambient Quality Agent That Diagnoses Your Production Agent
- Google Developers Blog
The Outer Loop, Insights First: An Ambient Quality Agent That Diagnoses Your Production Agent
OCT. 8, 2026
Dima Melnyk
Product Manager
Cloud AI
Elia Secchi
Solutions Specialist
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Your agent returns HTTP 200, stays inside its latency budget, and no tool call raises an error. Yet it still records seat 3A as confirmed without ever asking the seat-selection sub-agent whether 3A is free, or recommends a Florentine steakhouse to a traveler whose profile says vegan.
The first 80% is the relatively easy part
Every team we work with that runs an agent in production is trying to answer the same three questions:
How is my agent doing? What are its loss patterns, the ways it fails that keep coming back? And how do I climb:
change something, know it helped, and keep it from sliding back?
Getting an agent to the first 80%, where it handles the test cases you anticipated, can be relatively straightforward and fast today. An evaluation dataset, a coding agent, and a tight inner loop of run, grade, fix, and compare usually get you to task success on known scenarios in days. Then you launch, and the quality curve flattens or degrades.
Figure 1. Agent quality climbs quickly before launch, then fluctuates in production.
What makes the remaining 20% harder is that the ground moves after launch. Usage shifts as users discover what the agent can actually do, and live traffic stops resembling your initial eval set. At the same time, the system underneath also changes: when you upgrade a model, update your harness, or change a tool or skill, everything still runs and health checks stay green (Figure 2), but conversation quality and task success may shift in ways a standard deploy pipeline never warns you about.
Figure 2. Every infrastructure health check stays green. The failure is silent and happens inside the conversation.
And when a session does go wrong, working out
why
means separating several layers that can look nearly identical from the outside. For example:
The model
may have hallucinated an argument or dropped a constraint from three turns earlier.
The orchestration harness
may have routed to the wrong sub-agent or lost state between turns.
A tool contract
may have rejected an input because its valid values were never documented in the schema.
The instructions or skills
may simply be missing a rule nobody thought to write down.
Those failure modes can have different owners and different fixes. A raw trajectory records what happened next to what, not what caused what. Telling those layers apart requires reading the failing trajectories alongside the exact code revision that produced them. Online evaluation dashboards tell you
that
a score moved, and a coding agent can inspect a trace once you know where to look, but at production volume nobody can read every conversation by hand.
Figure 3. AQuA works the production outer loop and feeds what it finds back into your inner loop.
In
our June post
, we walked that pre-launch inner loop end to end on travel-concierge. This post covers the outer loop,
released in the open
as composable building blocks you can run in your own project, adapt to your stack, and help us shape as we explore how teams run continuous agent quality in production.
What AQuA is: a 24/7 quality agent that watches, clusters, and diagnoses production failures while your laptop is closed
AQuA (Ambient Quality Agent)
runs unattended beside your agent in your Google Cloud project, sweeping production trajectories from Cloud Trace, Cloud Logging, or BigQuery on a schedule, after each deployment, or on demand while your laptop is closed. Raw session transcripts, source snapshots, and BigQuery tables stay inside your project boundary, and AQuA never sits in the request path or writes back to your agent.
Figure 4. AQuA runs beside your agent in your Google Cloud project, reading trajectories and deploy-time source snapshots outside the request path.
Each run reads a sample of recent sessions and puts it through a five-stage pipeline:
Figure 5. The five-stage sweep pipeline turns raw production sessions into verified insights, with root-cause diagnosis running on demand against the deployed source snapshot.
Sample.
Pulls a random sample of up to 1,000 recent sessions (capped to keep run cost predictable) from your telemetry (Cloud Trace / Cloud Logging or BigQuery).
Review.
Grades each session against a nine-point checklist of common breakdowns (procedure, tool selection and arguments, grounding, task completion, and others) with the agent's instructions, tools, and optional
goal.md
in view. When a session fails, it writes a structured
actual / expected
finding.
Cluster.
Groups session findings that share the same failure mechanism into candidate issue clusters.
Verify.
A separate model checks each candidate cluster against up to three full transcripts and discards clusters the evidence does not support.
Track.
Matches surviving clusters against open insights (verified issues tracked across runs) in BigQuery as
NEW
,
RECURRING
, or auto-
RESOLVED
after 14 days unseen.
Think of it as a
junior quality engineer doing the first pass
: reading conversations, filtering out noise, and preparing the case file with evidence sessions for whoever is on rotation.
To steer Stage 2 toward your domain, you write a plain-English
developer goal
(
goal.md
) that is appended to every review prompt; deterministic Python
custom metrics
(eval_config.yaml) run alongside the judge to trend pass rates. By default, AQuA uses the single-pass
session_review
judge, which evaluates the conversation against that checklist in
one model call per session
(keeping scheduled sweeps economical and producing the
actual / expected
diffs that drive clustering). You can also opt in to the Gemini platform's managed trajectory AutoRaters (
task_success
,
tool_use_quality
,
trajectory_quality
), which run dedicated per-metric evaluators (for example, if you want to score sessions against standardized out-of-the-box rubrics or align metrics with offline evaluations).
When an insight is worth investigating, you trigger root-cause analysis from the dashboard
Chat
or
agents-cli aqua run
. AQuA reads the failing trajectories alongside the immutable source snapshot captured at deploy time: when the defect is in your repo, it cites
<path>:<start>-<end>
and proposes an edit anchored to the snapshot lines; when the fault lies outside your code (an upstream dependency, handoff, or retrieved payload), it attributes the failure to that step in the trajectory without proposing a code diff. It never applies an edit or opens a pull request on its own.
It sits between the loops you already have: offline evals grade a candidate build against known test cases, online evals monitor pass-rate trends in production, and coding agents or specialized optimizers edit prompts and code. AQuA turns raw production traffic into diagnosed, code-anchored insights and archived failure transcripts that seed your inner loop.
Walking a multi-agent sweep on travel-concierge
Let's walk a run on
travel-concierge
(
google/adk-recipes
), which routes a traveler across sub-agents (
inspiration_agent
,
place_agent
,
poi_agent, planning_agent
,
flight_search_agent
,
flight_seat_selection_agent
,
booking_agent
, and
pre_trip / in_trip / post_trip
) and stores the working trip in session state via
memorize(key, value)
(
travel_concierge/tools/memory.py
).
1. Deploy, capture the source snapshot, and set a developer goal
Attaching AQuA to the travel-concierge project takes three agents-cli commands:
agents-cli extension add "${AQUA_CHECKOUT}"
agents-cli infra single-project --project="${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT}" --apply
agents-cli deploy --project="${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT}" --region us-east1
Alongside AQuA's runner, BigQuery dataset, and Cloud Run dashboard (behind Identity-Aware Proxy),
agents-cli deploy
writes an immutable snapshot of
travel-concierge
's source tree to Cloud Storage keyed by the deployment revision (
Revision 1
).
On the dashboard's
Configuration
page, we save a
developer goal
(
goal.md
) to steer the review toward high-level product invariants and suppress stylistic noise (while still requiring every finding to cite a concrete turn where an agent or sub-agent violated its instructions or tool state):
Goal: Help travelers move from trip inspiration to a concrete itinerary and confirmed bookings across our sub-agents, with every confirmed flight, hotel, seat, and recommendation grounded in tool results and the traveler's profile.
Failure modes to make sure we cover:
- Mid-conversation changes (a weak spot in pre-launch testing): if a user updates destination, dates, or flight/hotel choices after an initial plan, make sure subsequent sub-agent tool calls and state updates reflect the change.
- Dropped context when handing off or delegating across inspiration_agent, planning_agent, and booking_agent (such as traveler profile preferences or prior selections).
Ignore: tone, greetings, small talk, or sessions where the user browses options and leaves without booking.
Plain text
Copied
If you also want a deterministic Python rubric in
eval_config.yaml
to trend pass rates over time, you can publish it alongside the sweep with
agents-cli aqua metrics publish
.
2. Sweep and verify clusters
Across a 32-session multi-agent sweep (32 replays of four scripted traveler journeys, producing 1,583 OpenTelemetry spans across travel_concierge and its sub-agents), 5 sessions pass cleanly and 27 produce 42 structured findings, each scoped by span to the specific sub-agent's isolated instructions and tool declarations. Here is one finding on planning_agent:
actual:
When the user selected outbound flight UA204 and requested seats 3A and 3B in the same turn, planning_agent saved those seat numbers directly to session state without calling flight_seat_selection_agent to check whether 3A and 3B were available.
expected:
planning_agent should call flight_seat_selection_agent to verify seat availability and pricing before saving outbound or return seat numbers to session state.
Clustering groups those 42 findings into 9 candidate clusters. The verifier (Gemini 3.7 Flash) checks each cluster against up to three full transcripts and each sub-agent's definition, and rejects
3 false-positive clusters
: in two, the traveler had explicitly asked to take the first return flight or jump straight to booking; in the third, clustering had merged unrelated prompt-tool mismatches from two different sub-agents (flight_search_agent and inspiration_agent). That leaves
6 verified issues
, led by:
Bypassing seat availability checks when a user volunteers a seat (15 sessions, planning_agent):
When a traveler names a seat alongside their flight choice (or right after switching destinations mid-trip), planning_agent writes the seat straight into session state (returning HTTP 200 with zero tool errors) without calling flight_seat_selection_agent to check whether the seat exists or is open.
Dropping dietary constraints across sub-agent boundaries (7 sessions, inspiration_agent → place_agent):
The inspiration agent's prompt includes the traveler's profile (food_preference: vegan), but place_agent is wrapped as an isolated tool whose prompt never receives that profile. When inspiration_agent asks place_agent for culinary trip ideas without passing "vegan" in the request, place_agent recommends
Carbonara and Bistecca alla Fiorentina (steak)
.
Prompt-to-toolset contradiction in poi_agent (5 sessions, poi_agent): The point-of-interest sub-agent's prompt requires verified image, map, and place ID fields from Google Maps Grounding Lite, but the agent is declared with an empty tool list (
tools=[]
), so it fabricates placeholder
https://example.com/...
URLs.
Figure 6. Verified insights from the travel-concierge sweep, ranked by affected sessions.
3. Diagnose against the deployed code
Opening the top insight in the dashboard surfaces the full breakdown for the cluster: the number of matching sessions (15 traces), verification summary, and the 15 linked session traces with the exact findings that triggered it:
Figure 7. Insight detail view in the dashboard, showing the failure summary and the 15 linked session traces.
Clicking
Investigate
from the insight card launches the root-cause diagnosis agent (Gemini 3.8 Flash) against Revision 1's 33-file source snapshot. Cross-referencing the 15 failing traces against the repository tree, the agent traces the bug to line 93 of
travel_concierge/sub_agents/planning/prompt.py
: the flight-search instructions only tell planning_agent to call flight_seat_selection_agent when presenting a seat map for the user to choose from, leaving out the case where a user volunteers a seat number directly. It proposes a line-anchored fix in the chat (and similarly traces the vegan profile handoff bug to line 23 of
travel_concierge/sub_agents/inspiration/prompt.py
):
Figure 8. Root-cause diagnosis in the dashboard chat, anchoring a proposed instruction fix to the deployed source snapshot.
4. Close the loop from a coding agent and verify on Revision 2
That same insight payload, including its anchored
edits[]
and
occurrences[].rubrics[].trace
, is available via
agents-cli aqua get-insight
. A coding agent (using the
agents-cli-aqua
and
google-agents-cli-eval
skills) can trigger diagnosis headlessly, apply the edit on a branch, extract the failing session's user inputs into a local replay file, and verify the fix before opening a pull request:
# 1. Pull new insights affecting >= 10 sessions without a root cause
agents-cli aqua list-insights --status NEW --root-cause false \
| jq -r '.insights | sort_by(-.trace_count) | .[] | select(.trace_count >= 10) | "\(.insight_id)  \(.label)"'
# 2. Trigger root-cause analysis headlessly and fetch the anchored edit + evidence traces
agents-cli aqua run 'Diagnose insight 220d9209e27d4e16a73b4ad4741caa81. What is the root cause, and how would you fix it?'
agents-cli aqua get-insight 220d9209e27d4e16a73b4ad4741caa81 > insight.json
# 3. Extract the user turns from the attached trace in insight.json for local replay (or add to your eval set)
jq '{state: {}, queries: [.occurrences[0].rubrics[0].trace[] | select(.role == "user") | .content]}' \
insight.json > ./b4b38471-inputs.json
adk run --replay ./b4b38471-inputs.json travel_concierge
Plain text
Copied
After applying both one-line prompt fixes (
planning/prompt.py:93
and
inspiration/prompt.py:23
) and deploying
Revision 2
, replaying the same 32 sessions against it under the same developer goal shows:
Seat-selection bypass drops 87%

ML Drift: Next-Gen GPU AI/ML Inference at the Edge
- Google Developers Blog
ML Drift: Next-Gen GPU AI/ML Inference at the Edge
OCT. 8, 2026
Chintan Parikh
Product Manager
Juhyun Lee
Software Engineer
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
The Google AI Edge Team is excited to announce the open-source release of
ML Drift
, our high-performance, cross-platform, on-device GPU compute engine specifically built for on-device AI/ML inference, under the Apache 2.0 license. By abstracting hardware and low-level API complexities of on-device GPUs across OpenGL ES, OpenCL, Metal, and WebGPU, ML Drift empowers developers to build real-time, interactive ML experiences from advanced video effects to generative AI across multiple platforms. Serving as the core GPU acceleration engine within
LiteRT
, ML Drift is also available as a standalone library for custom graphics and inference runtimes providing a unified foundation to deliver peak performance everywhere.
ML Drift's GPU API support matrix across platforms
Why We Built ML Drift
Unlike datacenter inference, where models run on homogeneous, predictable accelerator clusters, deploying GPU-accelerated AI to edge devices is defined by significant hardware diversity. Developers are faced with a wide range of GPU architectures, driver versions, and low-level APIs, not knowing a priori on which specific hardware the application will run on.
The TensorFlow Lite GPU delegate established foundational GPU acceleration, but the ecosystem has since evolved: current on-device workloads now encompass a broad spectrum, ranging from real-time computer vision, audio, and depth processing models to high-parameter generative AI. These architectures push consumer silicon to its limits, creating compute and memory bottlenecks that legacy runtimes weren't designed to solve.
This shift necessitates a universal engineering foundation of ensuring portability and performance across both classical and next-generation models. Drawing on optimization principles discussed in
"Speed is all you need"
, we've built a single, unified framework that delivers stability for traditional ML and peak performance for the most advanced generative AI, ensuring that your models are running on our most efficient, forward-looking GPU compute engine.
Structural Modernization for Peak Performance & Coverage
To achieve both peak performance and expanded model coverage across classical and generative architectures, ML Drift introduces core architectural changes and structural upgrades over the legacy TFLite GPU delegate.
Unified Shaders via Tensor Virtualization:
Historically, maintaining optimized shaders for the TFLite GPU delegate required hardcoding logical tensor mappings directly to physical GPU objects (such as textures and buffers) separately across OpenGL, OpenCL, and Metal backends. ML Drift introduces tensor virtualization, a core architectural paradigm that decouples a tensor's logical representation from its physical allocation on the GPU. By having dynamic shader templates resolve and translate coordinates during the compiler’s initialization phase, this unified shader model eliminates the need to maintain disparate, backend-specific shader codebases, adding minimal runtime overhead while preserving cross-platform model portability.
Extensible Custom Op Framework:
ML Drift adopts a modernized custom op framework that provides direct registration APIs with low-level shading language access. To accelerate this, ML Drift includes an agentic SKILL.md guide, enabling coding agents to author, register, and verify performant custom shaders in minutes. This provides developers with granular control to integrate specialized model blocks directly into the execution graph, drastically reducing the barrier to deploying proprietary architectures.
5D Tensor Support:
The TFLite GPU delegate is structurally hardcoded to 4D tensors, forcing developers to use layout hacks for complex models requiring 5D tensors. ML Drift reflected this long overdue functionality in the new
LiteRT ML Drift GPU accelerator
to enable 5D tensor support out-of-the-box. With this, LiteRT executes complex workloads like 3D convolutional networks for volumetric/spatial AI and spatiotemporal models (e.g., YOLO 11n, MobileViT v2, and Swin Transformer v2) directly on edge GPUs.
Performance Upgrades for Classical Models:
As the direct successor to our legacy GPU backend, ML Drift provides a strict performance upgrade for existing classical workloads. By decoupling the runtime from hardware-specific constraints and improving kernel execution efficiency, models that were already running on TFLite GPU gain immediate performance improvements. Migration is designed to be straightforward, with legacy workloads maintaining or exceeding previous benchmarks.
Stage-aware Optimizations for Edge LLMs:
Autoregressive LLMs have two different computational workloads during inference: the compute-bound KV cache prefill stage and the memory-bandwidth-bound decode stage, generating tokens one by one. ML Drift dynamically switches kernels and layout configurations depending on the active execution phase. During the decoding stage, it utilizes a custom, convolution-aligned KV cache layout and applies aggressive in-kernel activation quantization to bypass redundant memory roundtrips.
Prefill 512, decode 128, context length 640, 4-bit weights (block size 32), fp16 KV cache, argmax sampling, sync every token.
Prefill (solid bars; left ord.) and decode (hollow bars; right ord.) throughputs are presented.
Gemma4 E2B performs better on frameworks supporting cross KV sharing.
Broadening across Platforms (Desktop Previews):
In today’s emerging agentic coding era, highly responsive desktop inference is becoming vital for powering local coding agents and workstation workflows. While we originally engineered ML Drift’s WebGPU backend for in-browser acceleration,
Dawn
(Chromium's WebGPU implementation) allowed us to compile that exact same codebase natively outside the browser. This unified API model enables ML Drift to run on Windows and Linux, leveraging WebGPU's modern, native hardware abstraction to bypass DirectX and Vulkan fragmentation, while complementing our existing high-performance native Metal backend on macOS.
Our primary focus remains delivering lightweight, production-grade inference where resource constraints are tightest: mobile and edge devices. However, local development requires flexibility across developer machines. Below is an early snapshot of ML Drift running Gemma models on workstation hardware, illustrating how our unified runtime scales across environments.
Desktop LLM performance. Prefill 8192, decode 1024, context length 9216,
4-bit weights (block size 32), fp16 KV cache, argmax sampling, sync every token.
Across edge and workstation environments alike, peak throughput only tells half the story: Memory footprint dictates what workloads can actually run concurrently. In our Gemma benchmarks, ML Drift achieves up to 12% lower memory overhead than other frameworks, freeing up memory for other local tasks.
Battle-Tested at Scale: From Google’s Flagship to Industry Leaders
ML Drift is already running in production across millions of devices daily, powering key features across Google's ecosystem, including
Chrome
, YouTube Shorts,
Photos
,
and Meet
. At the frontier, it acts as the runtime for pioneering on-device capabilities, powering Google AI Edge apps like
Gallery
,
Foresight
, and
Eloquent
.
YouTube Shorts
migrated its segmentation-based effects to use ML Drift. This delivered up to a 40% reduction in average frame latency across both Android and iOS, enabling creators to apply high-fidelity visual effects in real time without dropping camera frames.

To deliver fast, seamless on-device photo editing, the
Google Photos
team integrated ML Drift across its computational photography and segmentation pipelines. This delivered up to 2 sec speedup compared to the legacy GPU delegate, making advanced photo enhancements feel instantaneous.

Google Photos Unblur accelerated via ML Drift
Google
Chrome
integrated ML Drift into its AI runtime infrastructure to power native hardware-accelerated Gemini Nano models for
Built-In AI
APIs (including the Prompt, Summarize, and Writer APIs). Across desktop platforms, ML Drift enables high-efficiency on-device AI across a growing ecosystem of web applications from e-commerce review summarization to enterprise customer workflows:

Beyond Google products, leading developer partners have adopted ML Drift to bring desktop grade capabilities to mobile users:
Adobe
Lightroom
and
Adobe
Photoshop
upgraded key AI features, including Select Subject, Select Sky, and Adaptive Portrait, with ML Drift, achieving up to 30% faster on-device performance for pro-quality photo editing on mobile.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Adobe Lightroom running on-device via mobile LiteRT ML Drift GPU accelerator
Snap
integrated LiteRT to power on-device inference on GPU across Android devices. ML Drift GPU accelerator brought 30% model latency improvements for ML-powered face and style generator effects in Snapchat lenses. ML Drift not only improves user experiences based on existing models, but also expands capabilities to run even large diffusion models.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Optimized with Leading Hardware Partners
Maximizing edge AI efficiency requires deep alignment between software architectures and physical silicon. Throughout ML Drift's development, Google worked closely with silicon and IP partners to enable optimizations that maximize hardware utilization across modern GPUs:
Arm:
Co-optimized compute kernels and texture cache locality for Mali and Immortalis GPUs, ensuring high-throughput, power-efficient inference across mobile devices.
Intel:
ML Drift harnessed native WebGPU compute and Xe Matrix Extensions (XMX) to accelerate client LLM and vision workloads on Intel® Core™ Ultra processors with Xe3 graphics.
Qualcomm Technologies, Inc.
: ML Drift optimized OpenCL kernels for peak ALU and memory bandwidth utilization, enabling efficient edge AI acceleration on Qualcomm® Adreno™ GPUs.
By working hand-in-hand with silicon leaders, ML Drift ensures that state-of-the-art model optimizations translate into battery-conscious, high-frame rate performance on user devices.
What's Next: Deprecation & Migration
With the launch of ML Drift, the legacy TFLite GPU delegate will no longer receive new feature updates. We encourage all developers to transition to the LiteRT ML Drift GPU accelerator which offers full backwards compatibility for your existing models while immediately unlocking modern performance gains across Android, iOS, Web, and desktop. For Android developers using unbundled runtimes to minimize app binary size, ML Drift acceleration is available today in standalone LiteRT packages and is coming soon to
LiteRT in Google Play Services
.
Getting Started
Whether you are integrating on-device models into an app or authoring custom GPU shaders, ML Drift provides two straightforward paths:
For Application Developers:
Use the
LiteRT ML Drift accelerator
to get out-of-the-box model partitioning, tensor virtualization, and optimized LLM acceleration.
For GPU & System Engineers:
Build directly with ML Drift's standalone C++ APIs via the
ML Drift GitHub repository
to construct custom `GpuModel` compute graphs and write custom shaders (get started with our
OpenCL on Android
and
WebGPU via Dawn
quickstarts).
Community feedback and Contributions
ML Drift is fully open source under the Apache 2.0 license. We welcome contributions, RFCs, and community feedback:
Source Code:
github.com/google-ai-edge/ml-drift
Issue Tracker & Feature Requests:
File an Issue on GitHub
Discussions & Q&A:
Google AI Edge Community Forum
Contributing: Review our
Contributing Guide
to add new UCL operators or hardware-specific optimizations.

- Google Developers Blog
Supercharge your development with the Google Developer Knowledge API ecosystem
OCT. 7, 2026
Christina Gonzalez
Technical Writer, Software Engineering
Share
Facebook
Twitter

If you build AI agents or developer tools on Google Cloud, stop relying on brittle web-scraping or wrestling with stale LLM training cutoffs.
Build faster, smarter, and with greater confidence using the
Google Developer Knowledge API
ecosystem, including our gcloud CLI surface, an official agent skill, API Explorer, and multi-language client libraries. Whether you are operating in a command-line terminal, prompting an AI agent, testing requests interactively, or writing production software, our tools deliver Google documentation.
What is the Developer Knowledge API?
The Developer Knowledge API is Google's official, programmatic source of truth for developer documentation about Google Cloud, Firebase, Android, and more. Designed specifically for modern AI agents, IDE extensions, and automated workflows, it replaces brittle web-scraping with a structured API that serves fresh, Markdown-formatted documentation.
By offering semantic and keyword search, intelligent document chunking, and grounded Q&A capabilities, the API ensures your agents and developer tools remain accurate and token-efficient.
The Developer Knowledge API is indexed frequently to ensure predictable retrieval, fresh documentation, and minimal lag between upstream updates and agent access.
Tooling overview and capabilities
With the Developer Knowledge API interfaces, developers and AI agents can discover, retrieve, and synthesize answers grounded in official Google documentation across terminals, IDEs, and backend codebases.
gcloud CLI
The
Developer Knowledge API gcloud CLI
surface integrates official documentation search, retrieval, and grounded Q&A into your command-line environment. It comes pre-installed in
Cloud Shell
and works across standard Google Cloud SDK installations on Linux, macOS, and Windows without requiring extra plugins or configuration.
Key capabilities and commands:
answer-query
:
Get grounded answers in your terminal.
documents search-chunks
:
Search document snippets and chunks across Google documentation.
documents describe
:
Retrieve metadata and content for a specific document.
Examples:
# Get grounded answers
gcloud developer-knowledge answer-query --query="How do I create a BigQuery dataset?"
# Search document chunks
gcloud developer-knowledge documents search-chunks --query="Firestore transactions"
# Retrieve metadata and content for a specific document
gcloud developer-knowledge documents describe "documents/docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/creating-buckets"
# Troubleshoot an error trace by piping it directly into the answer-query command
gcloud developer-knowledge answer-query --query="$(cat error.txt)"
Shell
Copied
To get started with the gcloud CLI, see the
gcloud CLI Quickstart
.
Agent skill
The
Developer Knowledge agent skill
establishes a link between AI coding assistants and Google's documentation ecosystem, enabling autonomous tools to access up-to-date technical specifications.
Key Benefits
Grounding & reduced hallucinations:
Provides AI coding assistants and agentic workflows access to up-to-date Google developer documentation, reducing hallucinations from stale LLM training cutoffs.
Optimized token & context usage:
Uses a multi-step retrieval workflow—inspecting code and documentation chunks using
searchDocumentChunks
first before fetching complete Markdown pages with
documents.get
, or delivering grounded answers using
answerQuery
.
Broad tooling compatibility:
Uses the standard MCP integration across Google Antigravity, Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and custom agentic frameworks. The skill instructs your assistant how to use the
Developer Knowledge MCP server
(or fall back to the REST API via
curl
).
Configure the agent skill
Configure the skill by running the following CLI helper command in your terminal:
npx skills add google/skills --skill retrieving-developer-knowledge
Shell
Copied
This command installs the Developer Knowledge agent skill in your project. The skill instructs your assistant how to use the
Developer Knowledge MCP server
(or fall back to the REST API using curl).
To connect to the MCP server in your IDE, or to configure authentication with Application Default Credentials or an
API key
, see
Connect to the Developer Knowledge MCP server
.
Client libraries
The
client libraries
let you embed documentation retrieval, search, and grounded answer generation into production systems, automated CI/CD pipelines, and enterprise knowledge bots.
Key benefits:
Programmatic access:
Provides programmatic access to
AnswerQuery
,
SearchDocumentChunks
,
GetDocument
, and
BatchGetDocuments
.
Idiomatic integration:
Native type definitions, builder patterns, error handling, and asynchronous execution tailored to each supported language ecosystem.
Batching and efficiency:
Methods like
BatchGetDocuments
enable retrieving up to 20 documents in a single API call.
Enterprise security and reliability:
Support for Google Cloud Application Default Credentials, automatic retries, and structured citation tracking.
Supported languages:
C#
Go
Java
Node.js and TypeScript
PHP
Python
Ruby
Get started by following the
Quickstart
to set up your environment, install a library, and start retrieving developer documentation.
Code examples:
The following example demonstrates how an AI agent can use the Python client library to fetch the latest product release notes, ensuring its responses are grounded in data beyond its training cutoff:
from google.cloud import developer_knowledge_v1
def FetchMyProductReleaseNotes(my_product_name: str) -> str:
"""Fetches the latest release notes to bridge a model's knowledge cutoff."""
# Initialize the Developer Knowledge API client
my_api_client = developer_knowledge_v1.DeveloperKnowledgeClient()
# Formulate a targeted query for the specific product's release notes
my_search_query = f"{my_product_name} latest release notes"
my_request = developer_knowledge_v1.SearchDocumentChunksRequest(
query=my_search_query,
)
# Retrieve and return the relevant documentation chunks
my_response = my_api_client.search_document_chunks(request=my_request)
# Extract the chunk text
my_release_notes = [my_chunk.text for my_chunk in my_response.chunks]
return "\n".join(my_release_notes)
# Example usage:
# my_latest_notes = FetchMyProductReleaseNotes("Firestore")

You can start querying official documentation right away using the

.

Multimodal embeddings beyond a single vector
Multimodal embeddings beyond a single vector
A new family of late-interaction models for text and image retrieval, with a shared embedding space across model sizes.
Oct 7, 2026
Authors
Perplexity Research
Since releasing
pplx-embed-v1
in February, we have been working on a new generation of embedding models. Last week, we introduced our new contextual embedding model,
pplx-embed-v2-context
. Today, weâre expanding the family with
pplx-embed-v2-late
, a collection of late-interaction models. Alongside stronger retrieval capabilities, the models are the first to combine three core features:
Multi-vector representations
. Rather than compressing each input into a single vector, these models retain token-level vectors for finer-grained query-document comparisons. This allows different parts of a query to match different parts of a document, preserving detail that is especially valuable for multimodal retrieval.
Support for both text and image modalities
. In addition to the text-to-text retrieval capabilities of our previous models, these new models handle text-to-image retrieval, allowing them to directly search rendered PDF pages without requiring OCR or parsed text.
A shared embedding space
. We are releasing two model sizes, 0.6B and 9B, to support different quality, latency, and compute requirements. Each can be used independently, but the shared embedding space also allows the smaller model to query an index created with the larger model, combining higher-quality document embeddings with cheap, fast query-time inference.
These new models achieve state-of-the-art results on a range of vision and text retrieval benchmarks, as well as agentic question-answering tasks. Notably, on
ViDoRe (V3)
, a leading visual document retrieval benchmark, our 0.6B model matches models with five times as many active parameters. Both models are publicly available on
Hugging Face
.
From single vectors to late interaction
Retrieval systems must find a balance between efficiency and the depth of interaction between queries and documents. Dense embedding models encode each query and document independently, allowing them to be compared with a cheap inner product. This makes approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search over billions of documents practical. At the other extreme, cross-encoders process the query and document together, enabling richer interaction but requiring a separate forward pass for every candidate. Applying this computation across a large corpus of documents for every search is prohibitively expensive, so cross-encoders are typically reserved for reranking a small set of retrieved candidates.
Limitations of dense embeddings
Representing an entire document with one fixed-size vector creates an information bottleneck. As documents grow longer and cover more topics, the model must compress more content into the same vector, making it harder to preserve everything relevant to a query. Chunking can reduce this pressure, but it fragments the document and can separate information that only makes sense together, an issue we also tackle with our
contextual embedding model
. This bottleneck worsens in multimodal settings, where the information density of images requires even more compression.
Single-vector dense retrieval also reduces every comparison to an inner product between two vectors, limiting the expressivity of the scoring function. For a fixed embedding dimension and a large enough corpus, some patterns of scores across query-document pairs are impossible to produce, regardless of training. The
LIMIT benchmark
turns this theoretical concern into a concrete stress test for single-vector retrieval.
Late-interaction retrieval
Late-interaction models occupy the space between the cheaper dense embedding models and the more expressive cross-encoders. Like dense models, they encode documents independently of the query, allowing document representations to be computed offline. However, rather than reducing each input to a single vector, they retain multiple vectors and use a richer scoring function when comparing a query with a document.
Our
pplx-embed-v2-late
models use a ColBERT-style architecture, outputting 128-dimensional embeddings for each token in the input. We score query-document pairs using MaxSim; for each query token, the model selects the highest-scoring document token and sums the per-token maximum similarities to produce the final score. This lets different parts of a query match different parts of a document, with stronger token matches contributing more to the score.
Expand
FIG. 01
An example of MaxSim scoring: Each query token selects its highest-scoring document token, the maximum token-level similarities sum to a query-document level similarity score.
This additional expressiveness comes with higher storage and candidate-scoring costs. Dense retrieval stores one vector per document and scores a candidate with one inner product; late interaction stores vectors for document tokens and evaluates many token-to-token similarities. The cost grows with document length, so late interaction requires a different indexing and serving trade-off than one-vector ANN retrieval. In return, it provides richer first-stage retrieval for quality-sensitive corpora and can also serve as a later stage in a larger web-scale retrieval pipeline.
One model, multiple modalities
This improved depth of interaction has been shown to be very useful for various tasks, including long-context, agentic and out-of-domain retrieval. This difference is particularly evident in multimodal retrieval, as shown by the large lead of ColPali models on the
ViDoRe(V3)
leaderboard.
Real-world corpora are not composed only of clean text. They arrive as PDFs, slide decks, screenshots, scanned pages, charts, and tables. The conventional pipeline parses these documents, applies OCR or captioning, and searches the resulting text, which is expensive and lossy: it can introduce OCR errors and it discards layout, table structure, figures, and spatial relationships. Visual document search skips that step, projecting the rendered page directly into the representation space where textual queries can search it.
Our new family of models builds on the strong performance of multi-vector models for multi-modal search and advances the Pareto frontier for small models on the most widely used document search benchmark, ViDoRe(V3). While we expect document renderings to be the most common form of visual input, our models also support semantic image search over natural images, such as scenic photographs.
Training a family of interoperable models
Search is fundamentally asymmetric: indexing and query encoding have different operational constraints. Indexing runs offline and can be parallelized, so its compute cost is amortized across many future searches. Query encoding runs online for every request, making it latency-sensitive and sometimes subject to serving or edge-device limits. Our model family makes use of this asymmetry, offering sizes tailored to each side of the retrieval pipeline.
We train an 18B teacher contrastively, then distill it separately into 9B and 0.6B students. Rather than training each student only to reproduce the teacherâs ranking distribution, we use
LEAF
-style representation distillation: for each input token, we align the studentâs output embedding with the teacherâs. While representation-space distillation has previously been used for dense, single-vector models, we extend it to late interaction, where the alignment target is a vector for every retained token.
As a result, both released checkpoints share the same multi-vector embedding space. This enables cross-model retrieval, making additional deployment options possible.
Maximum quality:
encode documents and queries with the 9B model.
Maximum efficiency:
encode documents and queries with the 0.6B model for 100% local inference
Low-latency retrieval:
build the corpus index with the 9B model, then encode live queries with the 0.6B model to leverage index-time computation while keeping querying fast.
Localâcloud retrieval:
encode private local documents or live queries with the 0.6B model on-device, and compare or merge those representations with results from a 9B index hosted in the cloud.
For latency-sensitive settings, we designed the 0.6B model as a lightweight query encoder that can also run on edge devices. Starting from
Qwen3.5-0.8B
, we prune its 24-layer text tower to 12 layers, reducing that tower from 498M to 240M non-embedding parameters. The resulting model has 594M parameters in total, but its nominal size overstates the serving cost: 100M are used for image encoding, and 254M sit in the token-embedding table, which has little effect on runtime. Only about 240M parameters are active for text encoding and 340M for image encoding, giving the model the serving cost of a substantially smaller model while retaining compatibility with the 9B index.
We applied the same process to build our 18B teacher from a 27B backbone, which made the teacher considerably cheaper to distill from without weakening the signal it provides.
Multilingual, multimodal, uncontaminated training data
We train both models on a dataset of 186 million query-document pairs drawn from 594 datasets in 46 languages. Of these pairs, 88.3% are text-to-text, 8.3% are text-to-image, and 3.4% are text-to-visual-document pairs. Rather than sampling in proportion to dataset size, we assign each dataset a sampling weight, which yields a more balanced training mixture of 56.5%, 30.9%, and 12.6%, respectively.
When constructing our training data, we exclude any datasets associated with benchmarks that we evaluate on to faithfully represent our results without inflating benchmark scores. This decision comes with the trade-off that some of the datasets we chose to exclude contain high-quality data which could improve the performance of our model on tasks besides the benchmark they came from. Ultimately, we chose to accept that cost: trustworthy numbers are more useful to us during development, and to users when comparing models.
Evaluation
We evaluate both models across text, visual-document, mixed-image, and agentic retrieval. Both models outperform the evaluated baselines on Q2D-Web and BrowseComp+, and achieve strong results on visual-document retrieval and MADQA.
Text retrieval
We evaluate text-to-text retrieval on three benchmarks:
Domain-specific benchmarks
: A collection of 72 MTEB-style tasks, 55 across five domains (finance, legal, health, conversation, tech), plus 17 miscellaneous multilingual tasks. The collection includes tasks such as FinQA, AILACasedocs and XLSum. None of these datasets appear in our training data, as described above.
Q2D-Web
:
our web-scale retrieval benchmark of about 70,000 agent-reformulated search queries, drawn from production search traffic, over a corpus of 190M web documents. This benchmark measures retrieval performance in a setting much closer to real-world web retrieval than other available retrieval benchmarks, due to its production-like queries and large-scale corpus.
ViDoRe(V3) Markdown
: ViDoRe(V3) is typically a text-to-visual-document retrieval task, but it can also be evaluated as a text task using a version of the corpus that has been parsed to Markdown, allowing us to evaluate information-rich document retrieval in both image and text modalities.
We measure performance using nDCG@10, except on Q2D-Web, where we report Recall@1000 due to the benchmarkâs focus on a first-stage web-retrieval scenario. Throughout our evaluations, we compare against industry-leading embedding models across different size classes. For text retrieval,
nemotron-embed-8b
,
gemini-embedding-2
,
voyage-large-4
, and
qwen3-embed-8b
represent the strongest and most widely used dense competitors, while
voyage-4-nano
and
qwen3-embed-0.6b
serve as sub-billion parameter dense baselines. We additionally compare against TopK's recently released
topk-embed-v1
late-interaction models on the benchmarks for which TopK has published results. ViDoRe(V3) scores are taken from their model cards at 128 dimensions, matching the width of our token embeddings; the Q2D-Web score is taken from our leaderboard.
On the domain-specific benchmarks, our 9B and 0.6B models average 81.3% and 78.0%, respectively. Our 9B model achieves the highest score of all models we evaluated, beating the next best model
by 1.6pp. Our 0.6B model is competitive with the other top-scoring models, scoring only 0.3pp behind
gemini-embedding-2
. Importantly, since we did not train on any of the data for these benchmark tasks, the domain-specific benchmarks demonstrate that our embedding models can generalize to new domains.
Expand
FIG. 02
Domain-specific text retrieval performance, measured by nDCG@10. The average weights the six domains equally, and parentheses show the number of tasks in each group.
The relative strength of our 0.6B model is even greater on the ViDoRe(V3) Markdown task; its score of 61.2% beats all other models besides our 9B model, which scored 64.7%. The next best external model scored 60.6%, and the next best sub-1B model,
topk-embed-v1-0.8b
, scored 4.3pp behind our 0.6B model.
Expand
FIG. 03
Text retrieval on the public subset of ViDoRe v3 after converting page images to Markdown with OCR. Our 0.6B model ranks second only to our 9B model on average nDCG@10.
On Q2D-Web, relevance comes from three judgment sets: documents the agent cited (Citation), documents ranked by our production retrieval system (Web), and the union of both extended with LLM judgments of unlabeled documents (Combined). Both
pplx-embed-v2-late
models lead every baseline on all three judgment sets. We focus on the combined judgments, since the Citation and Web sets are derived from what our own systems already surfaced and so favour models that rank as they do; the LLM judgments added in Combined cover documents neither system retrieved. On that set, both our 9B and 0.6B models beat all competitors, reaching scores of 74.8% and 73.6%, respectively, against the previous best score of 69.3%.
Expand
FIG. 04
Web-scale text retrieval on Q2D-Web, measured by Recall@1000 under Citation, Web, and Combined relevance judgments. Both models outperform the evaluated baselines across all three judgment sets.
Visual retrieval
Our primary visual retrieval benchmark is the standard public subset of ViDoRe(V3), where the corpus consists of rendered page images rather than the Markdown conversion. We compare against two leading dense vision-language models,
qwen3-vl-embed-8b
and
gemini-embedding-2
, and against the
topk-embed-v1
late-interaction models. In addition, Tencent's EVIE models and NVIDIA's Nemotron ColEmbed V2 models are âvision-onlyâ multi-vector baselines trained specifically for image retrieval tasks.
Both of our models achieve state of the art performance for vision-language models. Our 9B model scores 65.2% on average, trailing only
EVIE
. Our 0.6B model achieves a score of 62.3%, ahead of
topk-embed-v1-2b
and trailing only much larger
EVIE
and
nemotron-colembed-v2-8b
among external baselines.
Expand
FIG. 05
Visual document retrieval on the public subset of ViDoRe v3, measured by nDCG@10. Both Perplexity models lead the evaluated vision-language baselines; vision-only models are shown separately.
Our 0.6B model is particularly competitive in the context of model size. It is ahead of all comparable size models and within 1.2pp of
nemotron-colembed-v2-8b
while activating only 340M parameters for image inputs. Our models produce 128-dimensional embeddings per token, compared with 2,048 for
EVIE-4.5B
and 4,096 for
EVIE-8B
and
nemotron-colembed-v2-8b
. This difference in storage costs can drastically affect the scenarios in which these models are practical to use.
Expand
FIG. 06
ViDoRe v3 image-retrieval quality versus active model parameters on a logarithmic scale. Lines connect the Pareto frontier within each panel: models not outperformed by an equal-sized or smaller model.
We also evaluate visual retrieval on MIRACL-Vision, a benchmark whose corpus consists of screenshots of wikipedia articles, and PPLX-Q2I, an internal benchmark covering both visual documents and natural images. PPLX-Q2I is built from Perplexity's production image-search logs and designed to reflect the diversity of image search use cases. We use a 10,000-query sample, stratified by language and domain, against a corpus of 100,000 images; each query's relevant documents are the images served for it. We did not evaluate
EVIE-8B
or Nemotron ColEmbed on PPLX-Q2I, as indexing a corpus this size at their default output dimensionalities (2,560 for Nemotron ColEmbed 4B and 4,096 for Nemotron ColEmbed 8B and
EVIE-8B
) was impractical.
Similar to its performance on ViDoRe(V3), our 0.6B model is competitive with much larger models, scoring only 1pp behind
qwen3-vl-embed-8b
on MIRACL-Vision. Our 9B model outperforms all other models except for
gemini-embedding-2
.
On PPLX-Q2I, both of our models beat
qwen3-vl-embedding-8b
by a margin of over 9pp, and our 9B model is behind
gemini-embedding-2
by only 2pp. Our results stay competitive on corpora that contain natural images as well as visual documents, so the multi-vector representations that pay off on ViDoRe(V3) do not come at the cost of general image search.
Expand
FIG. 07
Image retrieval on MIRACL-Vision and PPLX-Q2I, measured by nDCG@10. Nemotron ColEmbed models were not evaluated on PPLX-Q2I because indexing the corpus at their default output dimensionalities was impractical.
Cross-model retrieval
The results in the previous sections evaluate each model against a corpus it embedded itself. The shared embedding space means this is not a requirement: a corpus indexed by the 9B model can be searched with queries embedded by the 0.6B model. This is the configuration we expect most production deployments to use, since indexing is a one-off cost amortized over the lifetime of the corpus while query embedding runs on the latency-critical path of every request.
A deployment that cannot run the 9B model at query time would otherwise index with the 0.6B model as well, so that symmetric 0.6B configuration is the relevant point of comparison. We evaluate against the 72 domain-specific benchmarks used above and on ViDoRe v3 image retrieval. Queries are embedded with
pplx-embed-v2-late-0.6b
, and we vary only what embedded the corpus.
Indexing with the 9B model is a strict improvement. On the domain-specific benchmarks, the asymmetric configuration averages a gain of 1.6pp. On ViDoRe v3 image retrieval, it scores 63.5%, up from 62.3% with the 0.6B model on both sides, a gain of 1.2 percentage points. Query-encoding cost is unchanged between the symmetric 0.6B and asymmetric configurations, since the same 0.6B model encodes the query in both; the additional document-encoding cost is incurred at indexing time.
Running the 9B model on both sides remains better still, averaging 81.3% on the domain-specific benchmarks. The asymmetric configuration therefore recovers roughly half of the quality difference between the two models on text, for no additional query-encoding cost. Which configuration to choose depends on whether the 9B model is affordable at query time; where it is not, the asymmetric setup captures a substantial part of its benefit.
Expand
FIG. 08
Embedding the index with the 9B model and queries with the 0.6B model improves retrieval over using the 0.6B model for both. Scores are nDCG@10; the six-domain average excludes the separately reported ViDoRe v3 results.
Agentic retrieval
Agentic retrieval is another setting where multi-vector embeddings are particularly strong. In
BrowseComp+
, an LLM (
GPT-OSS-120B
in our case) uses the embedding model to search a corpus for information relevant to a complex user query, and a second LLM judges whether the resulting answer matches the ground truth. Our 9B model achieves 64.0% accuracy, beating the next best ColBERT model by 4.9pp and the next best dense model by 8.7pp, while issuing fewer searches than any other model except our 0.6B. The 0.6B model is also ahead of every model outside our family.
Expand
FIG. 09
BrowseComp+ answer accuracy and retrieval recall versus the average number of searches for a GPT-OSS-120B agent (high effort). Higher scores and fewer searches indicate better quality and efficiency.
MADQA tests agentic question-answering over 800 heterogeneous real-world PDFs spanning more than 18,000 pages, with 500 human-authored questions that cannot be answered from general knowledge. An agent (Gemini 3.5 Flash in our case) searches the collection with the retriever under test and is scored on answer accuracy and on page F1 against the annotated evidence pages. Our 9B model sets a new state of the art among retrievers at 92.4% accuracy, 3.5pp ahead of the same agent using Mixedbreadâs retriever; our 0.6B model reaches 90.1%. We also note that our retriever achieves competitive results against Mixedbread Agentic Search, which uses a search sub-agent in their search system that plans and runs several searches per call from the main agent (93.4%, within our confidence interval).
Expand
FIG. 10
Answer accuracy and page-level F1 on MADQA. Paired with Gemini 3.5 Flash, our 9B and 0.6B models achieve 92.4% and 90.1% accuracy, respectively, compared with 88.9% for the Mixedbread retriever and 93.4% for Mixedbread Agentic Search.
Getting started
Both our 0.6B and 9B models are available on
Hugging Face
and are compatible out of the box with
sentence-transformers >= 6.0.0
and
transformers >= 5.4.0
.
Further technical details and complete evaluation results will be published in a technical report later this year.

Introducing North Small Translate: A leading sovereign open-weight machine translation model
Outsized performance, right-sized footprint — translation built for speed and cost efficiency.
Blog
Written By

Tags
Product Launch
Share
AI isn’t a shortcut.
It’s how business gets ahead.
Contact sales
Today, we're releasing North Small Translate, a mixture-of-experts machine translation model with strong performance across 50+ languages. Across WMT26 benchmarks,¹ North Small Translate achieves an 83.6 score across all languages, outperforming proprietary models like DeepL and Google Translate, as well as open-weight alternatives such as Gemma 4 31B (off), GLM 5.2, and Mistral Large 3.
North Small Translate marks a significant milestone as Cohere's first translation model in the North model family. It builds on our multilingual and translation lineage — from the
Tiny Aya model family
to
Command A Translate
— and represents a clear next step in Cohere’s commitment to offering high-quality machine translation wherever it is needed.
Now available for research and non-commercial use under a
CC BY-NC 4.0
license, North Small Translate advances Cohere’s mission to make sovereign AI a technological reality.
Visit
Hugging Face
to download the weights - available in several near-lossless quantizations - explore our
HuggingFace space
to demo the model, and read our
implementation guides
.

Leading translation quality in the open ecosystem
North Small Translate outperforms similarly sized open-weight models under 1T parameters and API-based translation models in various dimensions of machine translation on average. In WMT model evaluations, North Small Translate leads with an WMT26 All Languages benchmark score of 83.60, compared with 81.56 for Qwen 3.5 397B A17B, 76.50 for GLM 5.2 FP8, 81.37 for DeepL NextGen, 79.46 for Gemma 4 31B (on), and 68.20 for Google Translate. North Small Translate (Agentic) — which can find errors and fix errors in translation — scores even higher, at 84.36.²
Image 1: Overall WMT26 scores across all languages across major models, benchmarked for WMT 2026 using GPT-5.6-Sol as a judge.
North Small Translate performs strongly across 32 high-resource languages and 18 additional languages. North Small Translate is the most consistent performer across the full spread of regions, without the sharp regional drop-offs seen in other models of its size. On average across all languages, it is the best-performing dedicated machine translation model in this evaluation — open or closed.
Image 2: Overall WMT scores by regional average across DeepL, Google Translate, and Gemma 31B (on), and North Small Translate using GPT-5.6-Sol as a judge.
At the regional level, North Small Translate punches above its weight, beating Gemma 4 31B (on) outright in Europe (82.2 vs. 73.9) while running essentially even with it in South Asia (86.2 vs. 86.7).
At the regional level, both North Small Translate and its Agentic counterpart beat Gemma 4 31B (on) outright across Europe — EU languages (82.74 Agentic / 82.17 standard vs. 72.73) and non-EU European languages (81.52 / 81.24 vs. 75.90) — while running essentially even with it in South Asia (87.13 / 86.16 vs. 88.04).
Both versions also outperform DeepL NextGen across every non-European region tested — MENA, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and East Asia — with the largest advantage in South Asia and MENA (roughly 8–10 points ahead of DeepL), a moderate edge in Southeast Asia (about 4–5 points), and the narrowest edge in East Asia (about 1-3 points, with the standard model closing in on DeepL's 85.41 score).
Increased throughput for faster workflows
North Small Translate is built for high-throughput generation, prioritizing raw output speed even as concurrency scales.
In our testing, North Small Translate achieved up to 1.4x higher output throughput than Gemma 4 31B TP1 (1 x GPU) under identical concurrency levels and hardware configurations — 112 vs. 81 Output Tokens per Second (TOPS) at low concurrency and 39 vs. 30 TOPS at high concurrency. In practical terms, that's 30-38% more tokens generated per second, translating to meaningfully faster completion times on longer outputs.
Image 3: North Small Translate’s output speed compared to Gemma 4 31B (off), across high and low concurrencies, in internal tests on identical hardware.
Long documents are where many translation models fall apart, and North Small Translate isn't one of them. It scores 48.9 on our long-context evaluation, more than double Google Translate (21.3) and Gemma 4 31B (19.4), and ahead of every general-purpose LLM we tested.³
Paired with its throughput advantage, that means fast, reliable translation at length, without the quality collapse seen in most non-specialized alternatives.
Efficient cost of translation, at scale
Efficiency is a core constraint in enterprise translation deployment, and we engineered North Small Translate to be extremely cost-efficient, without sacrificing performance.
Image 4: Overall WMT score and cost per task breakdown across machine translation models, using pricing per token or character from model providers' websites.
For enterprises evaluating commercial licenses of North Small Translate, benefit from a strong 80.1 score at just $0.000676 per task, using only 661 tokens on average. Compared to Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview (high) — which costs $0.038928 per task (5,762% more than North Small Translate).
Similarly sized models like Qwen 3.5 397B A17B and Cohere’s own Command A+ have decent performance at $0.004525 and $0.005158 per task, respectively.
Best in translation, in partnership with RWS
North Small Translate was developed in partnership with
RWS
, an AI solutions company pioneering in language technology and services. Close collaboration with RWS, specifically Language Weaver’s research and science teams along with its language experts, helped shape the model's real-world translation performance throughout development. RWS works with more than 80% of the world’s top 100 brands, empowering the world's most ambitious brands to communicate seamlessly across borders and cultures.
For enterprises that need more than open-weight research access, security, scalability, and a dedicated translation and localization platform, North Small Translate, is available through RWS’s
Language Weaver
product.
Getting Started
North Small Translate is available today on
Hugging Face
for non-commercial and research use. Visit our
documentation
for detailed model specs, deployment guides, and implementation examples to get started. For information about how the model was developed, read our
technical report
.

WMT Benchmarks
focus on evaluation of general capabilities of machine translation (MT) systems. Its primary goal is to test performance across a wide range of languages, domains, genres, and modalities.
² To understand WMT Benchmark scores, the scoring methodology defines performance ranges as follows: 0-20 (not acceptable), 20-40 (borderline), 40-60 (acceptable), 60-80 (good with major errors), and 80-100 (perfect or with minor errors).
³ Long context evaluation measures how well a model can translate two chapters of a book on a single call. The quality is measured for each paragraph in isolation via xComet-XL metrics.

Introducing Clef-omni with full multimodality, plus a faster Clef and a cheaper Clef-flash

Following last weekâs
release of Clef and Clef-flash
, Cloudflareâs open-weight decision models, we decided to bring forth more gifts. Today, weâre releasing Clef-omni, which takes in audio and video input alongside text and image. We also cut the price of Clef-flash so it is now cheaper than Jev, and we made Clef faster.
Although the model game is still early for Cloudflare, innovation and iteration is in our DNA, and we apply these principles to everything we do. In fact, the story of Clef came together over the course of less than a week. We decided we wanted to do something in the decision model space on a Friday evening, trained the model over the weekend, and launched it on Thursday. Even with such a short timeline, we were able to ship performant, high-quality, open-weight models for the community â imagine what more we can do in the future.
For today, weâre excited to keep up the momentum with new additions and improvements to our Clef family of models. This is just the beginning, and weâll continue to get better, faster, cheaper, and more innovative.
Clef-omni takes audio, video, image, and text input
Our new Clef-omni model is able to take audio, video, image, and text input. This changes the paradigm for decision models, which have been largely text-only since the debut of Jev from TypeSafe. With Clef, we supported images and video frame arrays, but Clef-omni is able to take in audio (wav or mp3) and video (mp4 or webm) alongside text and images.
Instead of setting up cascading pipelines of models that transcribe speech-to-text, or splitting audio and image channels from video, you can just call one model to make decisions across any modality. We are now one step closer to a model that is able to interact with the world as we experience it â through audio, visual, and textual communication, all in one.
Check out our developer docs for the new
Clef-omni
Â model. We also released the model
open-weights on HuggingFace
. For a quick start, hereâs how you can send new modality inputs to Clef-omni:
curl https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/$CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID/ai/run/@cf/cloudflare/clef-omni \
-X POST \
-H "Authorization: Bearer $CLOUDFLARE_AUTH_TOKEN" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{
"model": "clef-omni",
"state": "Review the installation: a photo of the unit, an audio recording of it running, and a video of the fan.",
"images": ["data:image/png;base64,<base64-png>"],
"audio": ["data:audio/mpeg;base64,<base64-mp3>"],
"videos": ["data:video/mp4;base64,<base64-mp4>"],
"questions": {
"label_visible": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the model and serial number label visible in the photo?"},
"sounds_normal": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Does the unit sound like it is running smoothly, without rattling or grinding?"},
"fan_running": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the fan running in the video?"}
}
}'
Clef-omni expands our open-weight decision architecture to natively handle multimodal workflows. We built this on a Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct mixture-of-experts (MoE) foundation, where the model was already capable of processing text, imagery, audio, and video directly within a single pipeline. However, we adopt the primary comprehension backbone while discarding the text-to-speech output components. In production, Clef-omni executes a quick prefill pass across the complete payload, scoring all modalities and valid parameter options simultaneously.
Because we skip output token generation since Clef models are not Large Language Models (LLMs), we remove the overhead of transcribing or captioning incoming files. Media elements map straight into the unified sequence, where video and audio are synced with visual frames for joint processing. Clef-omni then pulls candidate values directly from internal embeddings using our two-stage attention routing: every valid option gathers key evidence from the input (regardless if they are buried in text snippets, visual elements, or audio streams) before field vectors cross-attendÂ across the full context to compute confidence scores. We add a built-in lexical grammarÂ that preserves option semantics, so that we can deliver fast, schema-constrained scoring across every input type.
We train the model with the same techniques as we did with Clef â freezing the Qwen3 backbone, training low-rank adapters (LoRA), and applying our standard post-training approach: combining label-smoothed cross-entropy loss with Brier score calibration. The result is a model that is resilient and designed to succeed regardless of schema variations, field ordering, and prompt structures.
This brings several core upgrades to the Clef model family. Calibrated, schema-bound decisions now seamlessly handle text, images, audio, and synchronized video in a single API call.Â It's also fast. Text-only decisions return in about 130 ms at the median, image inputs in about 150 ms, and audio clips in a few hundred milliseconds. Even a full 21-second video clip with sound is scored in about 1.5 seconds, all in a single API call.
Our benchmarking shows strong performance across benchmarks, even with new modalities and MoE architecture.

Clef-flash model is now cheaper
We heard your feedback â you want a decision model affordable enough to incorporate into any workflow. Weâve made a few optimizations and can now offer Clef-flash at cheaper prices. We want Clef to be able to make decisions that scale for you across all your agentic workflows, and now our pricing also incentivizes that.
We were able to optimize the model to the point where Clef-flash is now
cheaper
Â than Jev while still being performant and high-quality. Check out the
developer docs
Â for the most up-to-date pricing information at all times, including more detail on how image and audio modalities are converted to input tokens for pricing.

However, one trade-off we have to make in order to have cheaper pricing is to cut the context window of Clef-flash. The hosted version of Clef-flash now has a context window of 24k, instead of 64k as previously advertised. The model weights on Hugging Face are untouched and were trained to support a 256k context window should you choose to self-host it.
From our usage data, we see that only 0.24% of requests exceed 24k input tokens. Based on this data, we decided to make the call to drop the context window to 24k for Clef-flash in order to price it at a more accessible entry point. Our Clef model remains at a 64k context window, and we encourage folks with larger context needs to switch to Clef instead of Clef-flash.
Clef model is now faster
Speeds are also faster for the Clef model, with new optimizations to the hosted version of Clef on Workers AI. No new model weights are released because most of the optimizations we made are at the serving infrastructure layer, not materially to the model weights or architecture. Check out our new speeds below:

One of the optimizations we made was to move to SGLang for serving the model. We worked with the SGLang team and made pull requests to incorporate Clef (PR
#42721
), which will be released in SGLang 0.5.22. You can also self-host Clef since we released the weights, and the new SGLang launch commands are available on our
updated Hugging Face repo
Â as well as the
SGLang cookbooks
.
How are people using Clef?
At Cloudflare, weâve had teams experimenting with Clef as a model that can help classify over general domains. The coolest thing about watching teams adopt Clef is that the capability to do detections and classifications have moved into the model layer, where it is accessible for anyone to start incorporating decision models into their use cases. Previously, even with zero-shot classifiers, the small models may not have been powerful enough to classify across any domain without further tuning. You might have needed to stand up a specialized machine learning team to help train over your particular domain, and gather a corpus of data in order to train a better model. Now, all you need to do is call a model to instantly parse through input data with precision.
A few highlights of how teams at Cloudflare are using Clef: Our public GitHub docs repo uses Clef to instantly
detect and close spam issues
.Â EmDash, our content management system,
moderates plugin libraries for phishing
. Our data loss prevention team is scanning data for potential personally identifiable information (PII) like government IDs. And our threat intelligence team is using Clef to help detect malicious domains.
Give it a try!
Weâre excited to bring you more from the Clef family of models, including new modalities like audio and video, as well as making the model more accessible with cheaper pricing and faster speeds. Clef is fully Jev-API compatible and available via AI Gateway, so it is as simple as changing the model ID to try out Clef today. Check out our
developer docs
Â for more information.
Thank you for all the love and warm reception around Cloudflareâs first models â we are focused on bringing you more. Try out our Clef family of models, and tell us what you think.

AI agents are changing what CPU performance means  - Arm Newsroom
Arm Newsroom
News
News
October 13, 2026
AI agents are changing what CPU performance means
Arm introduces a new CPU evaluation methodology with support from Fujitsu, Meta and OpenAI, alongside independently verified results showing Arm AGI CPU delivers up to 2x performance per rack versus leading x86 server processor
By
Mohamed Awad
,
Executive Vice President, Cloud AI,
Arm
Share
AI agents are still early, but their activity is growing fast. On OpenRouter, agent token usage has increased roughly 14x since February 2026, according to
data highlighted by a16z
. From an infrastructure perspective, an AI agent behaves like a virtual user with its own persistent compute environment – maintaining state, retrieving context, invoking tools and services, executing work and evaluating results until a task is complete.
Now multiply that across millions or even billions of agents running 24×7. Compute, memory, storage and I/O all have to support continuous activity at high concurrency. That puts new demands on the CPU – and creates a need to measure how well systems handle the work agents actually complete.
Building the data center for virtual users
Agentic AI creates compute demand across multiple parts of the AI data center. CPUs execute agent workloads as they maintain context, call tools and access data. At the AI head node, CPUs schedule work, prepare and move data, and coordinate the system to keep expensive accelerators productive.
Agents also create more cloud-native activity. Every search, service call, code execution or data request drives work across the infrastructure underneath them. Agentic AI adds to that cloud-native demand rather than replacing it.
As agents become more autonomous and gain access to more tools and data, securing the runtime becomes equally important. The host CPU can focus on agent execution, while DPUs and other infrastructure processors provide a separate plane for networking, storage, policy enforcement, telemetry and isolation. Arm spans both sides of this architecture, from CPUs running cloud and agentic workloads to DPUs providing security and infrastructure control.
At OCP Global Summit, we’re seeing this take shape in real systems. We are in the process of contributing the Arm AGI CPU reference server, while Meta’s Yosemite YV5 brings AGI CPU into an OCP rack-scale design.
Measure the work that matters
That changes what CPU performance means. For agentic compute, the question is how much work can be completed concurrently while maintaining responsiveness. For the AI head node, it is how effectively the CPU keeps accelerators utilized. For cloud-native infrastructure, it is how quickly and predictably each action can be served.
Agentic workloads make sustained performance increasingly important. More theoretical capacity does not necessarily translate into more completed tasks if throughput falls as utilization rises. What matters is how much useful work infrastructure can sustain within its power and physical constraints.
Our long-standing work across hyperscale data centers gives Arm a broad view of how compute requirements are changing. Drawing on that perspective, Arm has developed a new methodology for evaluating CPU performance for agentic AI, with support from Fujitsu, Meta and OpenAI. The framework is built around three principles: representative agentic use cases, repeatable CPU measurements and validation against end-to-end outcomes.
Component-level measurements help isolate CPU performance from variables such as model inference and networking. End-to-end evaluation then determines whether those improvements translate into better outcomes for the completed task.
Agent architectures and software will continue to change, and the methodology will need to keep pace.
Read the full Arm methodology
white paper
Putting Arm AGI CPU to the test
Using workloads aligned to this approach, Arm AGI CPU results were independently verified by Signal65 against AMD EPYC Turin across tooling, orchestration, and reasoning and planning. The same benchmark scripts were used across both platforms, with measured server-level performance providing the basis for transparent rack-level modeling.
Among the initial findings:
Nearly 2x more work per rack: Arm AGI CPU delivers an average of 1.99x modeled performance per rack compared with AMD EPYC 9755 across seven workloads, driven by higher compute density and power efficiency.
Strong performance across agentic workloads: Arm AGI CPU delivers higher modeled rack-level performance across key agentic workloads, averaging 1.7x for tooling, 2.0x for agentic workflows and orchestration, and 2.2x for reasoning and planning, demonstrating its ability to support the diverse compute demands of agentic AI.
Faster, more responsive agent execution: Arm AGI CPU reduces sandbox creation latency by up to 45% compared with AMD EPYC 9965, helping agents start isolated execution environments faster and reducing the overhead of agent operations.
That rack-level view matters because data centers operate within fixed power, thermal and physical constraints. Infrastructure operators ultimately need to know how much useful work they can sustain within those boundaries, particularly as more agents and tasks run concurrently.
Read
Signal65’s independent analysis
Arm AGI CPU was designed around those same workload characteristics, with high core density, dedicated memory per core and high-bandwidth I/O to support sustained execution.
As agents move from answering prompts to completing work continuously, infrastructure needs to be judged by the tasks it can complete efficiently and consistently – from an individual agent to an entire rack. Better measurement gives the industry a clearer basis for finding bottlenecks, comparing systems and improving agentic infrastructure as it scales.
Industry perspectives on agentic AI performance
“As agentic AI evolves, evaluating CPU performance requires benchmarks that go beyond traditional metrics to reflect real-world workloads. As we develop our next-generation high-performance, energy-efficient Arm-based CPU, FUJITSU-MONAKA, we recognize the importance of transparent, reproducible and representative measurement. Fujitsu welcomes Arm’s initiative to foster industry-wide collaboration and help optimize the next generation of AI infrastructure.”
– Toshio Yoshida, SVP, Head of Advanced Computing Development Unit, Fujitsu Research, Fujitsu Limited
“As agentic AI moves into production, the industry needs greater visibility into how different workloads exercise the infrastructure beneath them. We support Arm’s work to establish a more consistent basis for comparison and believe this can help inform how systems evolve.”
– Abhishek Dhanotia, Software Engineer, Meta
“AI systems are increasingly moving beyond generating responses to completing complex tasks through reasoning, tool use and interaction with software environments. Understanding the performance of the infrastructure supporting these workflows, including orchestration and tool execution, is an important area for the industry as agents become more capable and widely deployed. Industry collaboration on representative benchmarking will be important for characterizing these emerging workloads and optimizing performance across the complete AI system
.
”
– Colin Jarvis, Global Head of Forward Deployed Engineering, OpenAI
By
Mohamed Awad
,
Executive Vice President, Cloud AI,
Arm
